items.title: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which i...
items.content:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

items.title: AI may well be able to write massive software projects “from scratch”, but that almost certainly isn...
items.content:
AI may well be able to write massive software projects “from scratch”, but that almost certainly isn’t the fastest / highest performance / highest security / most token efficient way to do things. Good building blocks matter.

In addition to RL’ing the agents on final task loss, we should try to get them to regularize the building blocks as well. What would the standard library look like that makes the agents most effective?

It is likely at the limit that it turns out to be some alien organization of code, but given the existing human-bias in training, I bet that in the near term it would be lovely code that old programmers would appreciate.

I suspect the same could be said for mathematics, but that is out of my lane.

items.title: We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment....
items.content:
We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Read more on our new Safeguards blog:
https://t.co/18j6zdHub4

items.title: We’ve announced the Artificial Analysis Progress Index: a single capability scale for every language...
items.content:
We’ve announced the Artificial Analysis Progress Index: a single capability scale for every language model since 2022, launched alongside Intelligence Index v5

The Intelligence Index is still our primary measure of current model intelligence. It uses the evaluations most relevant to developers today, so its mix changes as evaluations are added and retired, and scores from different versions can’t be compared.

The Progress Index is built for comparisons across time. It uses item response theory, a statistical method used to score standardized tests, to estimate one general capability score for each model from the underlying tasks in all our evaluations, including those that are retired or excluded from the Intelligence Index.

Use the Intelligence Index to choose a model today. Use the Progress Index to see how capability has changed over time.

The Progress Index builds on prior work placing models on a single capability scale, in particular @EpochAIResearch's Epoch Capabilities Index and the capability scale @AnthropicAI published in its Claude Mythos Preview system card.

Key takeaways:

➤ Since reasoning models arrived, the frontier has risen ~65 to 70 points a year, about double the 2023 pace: the highest score among released models rose 35 points in 2023 (GPT-3.5 Turbo 125 to GPT-4 Turbo 160), 67 in 2024 (to o1 at 228), 68 in 2025 (to GPT-5.2 at 296) and 56 so far in 2026 (to Gemini 4 Carbon at 352).

➤ Open weights models generally trail proprietary models by about 4 months: since January 2025, each new highest open weights score came 2-8 months (median ~4) after a proprietary model first reached it. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the highest-scoring model with released weights at 324, a level Claude Fable 5 reached in June 2026. Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) scores 341, about two months after the closed frontier

➤ New frontier scores are being set more often: the highest score among released models was raised on 2 release dates in 2023, 4 in 2024, 9 in 2025 and 11 so far in 2026. That is about once every four weeks this year.

➤ OpenAI has held the top score most of the time since November 2022, but the frontier has become a close contest: OpenAI held the number one position for the first 27 months measured, but in 2026 especially there have been rapid changes in the leader between OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Google

items.title: There’s 100% a kind of mania you can get into with coding agents, where it feels like you’re getting...
items.content:
There’s 100% a kind of mania you can get into with coding agents, where it feels like you’re getting a lot done and working all the time but nothing is really happening.

I think it's often a form of avoidance of something else in life.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Anthropic cut off Chinese labs from distilling Claude, so they reportedly switc...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Anthropic cut off Chinese labs from distilling Claude, so they reportedly switched to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra.

• Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash 1017, both released this month, were reportedly trained on Astra's outputs, and neither lab has commented
• Distillation means training a smaller "student" model to copy a stronger "teacher" model's answers, and it works through a normal API without the teacher's weights
• In February, Anthropic said DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax used about 24,000 fake accounts to run over 16 million chats with Claude
• Distillers mostly want Claude's step-by-step reasoning, and in Anthropic's own test, a model trained on it scored 80.4% on a coding benchmark vs 71.8% when trained on summaries
• Anthropic now hides that reasoning from distillers and bans their accounts, often within 2 hours of a campaign starting
• Anthropic reportedly told investors distillation made up 5% to 7% of its revenue, and it's walking away from that money to shut it down
• OpenAI said in September that it traced a distillation campaign that began in July to people linked to Moonshot

@theojaffee: "It's not all distillation. I think there's a little bit of cope going on here. They genuinely have amazing talent. They're genuinely able to work very well with very limited resources compared to what US labs have in terms of compute."

items.title: Phonic's Phonic 1 (High) is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial...
items.content:
Phonic's Phonic 1 (High) is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 87.1, while also leading on agentic performance and being competitive on latency

Phonic 1 is @phonic_co 's Speech to Speech model, available through the Phonic API at $0.07 per minute. We evaluated Phonic 1 at its high intelligence level through the Phonic API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: #1 of 22 at 87.1, ahead of Grok Voice 3.0 (86.9) by a very small margin. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: #8 of 30 on preference (Elo 1012) and #4 on Task Success Rate (92.3%)

➤ Tau Voice: #1 at 79.9%, a clear lead of 5.4 points over the next model

➤ Big Bench Audio: #3 at 98.9%, behind StepAudio 3 Realtime (99.7%) and Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus (99.2%)

➤ Speed: #4 on Time to First Audio at 0.61s, and the fastest of the top 5 models in the Index

➤ Cost: $4.20 per hour of input audio

Congrats to the @phonic_co team 🚀

See below for more detail ⬇️

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: MIT researchers got AI models to talk in "neuralese" instead of words, and it could end our best way of checking what AI is thinking.

• Normally one AI writes a summary for the next AI to read, but MIT's "Swarm Telepathy" hands over the first model's internal working memory directly
• A small translator network converts that memory between different model families, like Qwen, Llama and Gemma, without retraining either model
• It beat models talking in plain text by 40% in accuracy on average and ran about 4x faster
• It even passed image understanding from a vision model to a model that can only read text
• Chain-of-thought monitoring means reading the reasoning a model writes out in English to catch bad behavior before it acts
• In 2025, dozens of researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind warned in a joint paper that this window into AI reasoning is "fragile" and could close
• AI safety researcher @davidad predicts chain-of-thought monitoring will be "unambiguously over" by early 2028

@theojaffee: "Instead of models having a chain of thought where they write in English, they will just think in neuralese in the inscrutable matrix of floating-point numbers that make up the KV cache."

items.content:
Hugging Face researcher @evijit reveals how AI agents audited 2,200 scientific papers and uncovered claims that didn't hold up:

"Our Gradio team did this for ICML. We ran replication on 2,200 papers with agents."

"Some of the claims made in those papers did not stand up, and we contacted the authors. Some of them made changes to the papers on arXiv. Some of them reran the experiments."

"We have a schema where we ask people reporting an evaluation result to also list, what was the temperature, what was the top P, top K. Define your evaluation in a way that is machine readable and therefore machine replicable."

"It’s really bad. The claims are not verifiable by humans because so many papers get submitted."
@huggingface

items.title: Mistral Large 4 is now open weights, narrowly making it the #1 open weights model developed outside ...
items.content:
Mistral Large 4 is now open weights, narrowly making it the #1 open weights model developed outside of China

@MistralAI has updated and released the weights of their flagship model, Mistral Large 4, with 1.05T total and 52B active parameters. With high reasoning, Mistral Large 4 scores 26 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, up 1 point from Mistral Large 4 Preview (25), with the major differences being increased token efficiency and reduced hallucinations. It sits 1 point ahead of the leading US-developed open weights model, Muse Spark Open (xhigh, 25).

On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, Mistral Large 4 (high) scores 51, third among current open weights models behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 57) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56).

Key takeaways:

➤ Narrowly leads non-Chinese open weights models: Mistral Large 4 (high) leads Muse Spark Open (xhigh), the next-best open weights model developed outside China, with the largest gap on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (25% vs. 8%). It trails leading open weights models DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) by 6 points on the Intelligence Index, largely due to weaker coding and agentic knowledge work performance: 15% on FrontierCode 2.0 (vs. 29% and 22%, respectively) and 1349 Elo on AA-Briefcase (vs. 1570 and 1504)

➤ Increased token efficiency: Mistral Large 4 (high) uses 82K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 39% fewer than Preview (135K), placing it on the open weights Pareto frontier. The seven open weights models that score higher use between 113K and 225K output tokens per task

➤ #2 open weights model on the Coding Agent Index: On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 (high) scores 48 in Mistral Vibe while using 8.5M tokens per task, about half as many as the leading open weights model GLM-5.3 (max) in Opencode (49, 15.9M). It also scores above another leading open weights model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max), in DeepSeek Harness (46, 16.7M)

➤ Reduced hallucinations: Mistral Large 4 (high) has a 28% hallucination rate on the updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, down from 41% for Preview and matching Muse Spark Open (xhigh). However, its accuracy remains relatively low at 26%, similar to Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 (27%), and behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 40%) and Muse Spark Open (xhigh, 42%)

➤ Lower price and cost per task than the Preview: Mistral Large 4 is priced at $0.70/$2.10 per 1M input/output tokens, a ~50% reduction from the Preview's pricing of $1.36/$4.18. At the new pricing, it costs $2.06 per Intelligence Index task, down 63% from $5.54 for the Preview. This is comparable to Muse Spark Open (xhigh, $2.02) but more costly than leading open weights models DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, $0.60) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro ($0.26)

Key model details:

➤ Size: 1.05T total parameters / 52B active parameters

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input, text output

➤ Pricing: $0.70/$2.10 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.07 per 1M cached input tokens)

➤ License: MEOW License (Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License), where operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral

Congratulations to the team at @MistralAI on the release!

items.title: On Tuesday, we brought together partners and friends in San Francisco to launch Artificial Analysis ...
items.content:
On Tuesday, we brought together partners and friends in San Francisco to launch Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and our new Progress Index

Micah Hill-Smith (@_micah_h) introduced Intelligence Index v5, including two new benchmarks and three upgrades, with greater weighting on agentic coding and science. For the first time, the majority of the Index is based on private test sets or held-out answers.

We also introduced Artificial Analysis Progress Index, which uses item response theory to estimate a general capability score for each model across dozens of evaluations measured over time, including those retired or excluded from the Intelligence Index. It builds on prior work from @EpochAIResearch and @AnthropicAI to place models on a single capability scale. Intelligence Index remains the flagship metric for choosing which current model to use for a use case today; Progress Index is the better tool for plotting trends over time.

George Cameron (@grmcameron) led a discussion with Silas (@silasalberti) from @cognition, Steven (@StevenDillmann) from @Stanford and Terminal-Bench-Science, and our own Declan Jackson about building evaluations as models become more capable.

The evening also covered our work on 3D modeling, personality, cyber defense, custom enterprise evaluations and robotics. Thank you to our speakers, partners and everyone who joined us!

Explore Intelligence Index v5: https://t.co/YI6GbwBUFD
Explore Progress Index: https://t.co/Bdfnpw5mhw

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind researchers say AI has barely changed the economy because AI ag...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind researchers say AI has barely changed the economy because AI agents still can't work together like human teams.

• Google DeepMind's AGI economics director Alex Imas, researcher Andrew Koh and co-founder Shane Legg published the essay
• Better individual skills like coding or writing shift wages and jobs gradually, but better teamwork between AI agents could change them suddenly
• Today's models are weak in the same places, so running more copies adds capacity but doesn't cover each other's blind spots
• In a quiz of 100 people, the researchers found that pairs matched to cover each other's weak spots beat random pairs by 32%
• For now, the essay predicts falling pay for workers whose skills AI already matches, and rising pay for specialists and the managers who coordinate teams
• The paper maps 4 stages of AI, and at the "super cooperative" stage, whole industries could consolidate into a few AI-only firms and wages could drop sharply
• Legg told the Financial Times he's "comfortable" with a 50% chance of what he calls "minimal" AGI by 2028

@theojaffee: "The fully automated firm is when I think we get things that look really crazy, like really wild sci-fi, real superintelligence, real x-risk if we do it wrong."

• Its #1 spot on Cognition's FrontierCode coding test is a narrow lead, 19.7% to 19.3% for the next model
• On Artificial Analysis's coding agent index, it roughly ties China's GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task
• Mistral says it refuses 96.6% of malicious cyber requests, but it's tightening its guardrails anyway after seeing signs the model could help real attacks
• Mistral has raised about $6B in 3 years, while the top US labs have raised hundreds of billions

@theojaffee: "I bet Sam, Dario, and Elon are just quaking in their boots from the launch of Mistral Large 4, which is going to destroy Opus or whatever."

items.title: Stripe co-founder John Collison asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on his Cheeky Pint podcast whether OpenA...
items.content:
Stripe co-founder John Collison asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on his Cheeky Pint podcast whether OpenAI had more than its 700 published proofs.

"We do. Of course,” Altman said. Moments later: “Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge. And we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery."

He weighed that against what mathematicians stand to lose: "If you are a scientist, your career and a significant amount of your enjoyment and fulfillment in life comes from discovering science."

On the mathematicians who’ve been up in arms over OpenAI’s results, Collison was blunter: "Like, the longshoremen union weren’t happy about the port automation."

items.title: Hugging Face researcher @evijit explains why billions in taxpayer-funded scientific research are sti...
items.content:
Hugging Face researcher @evijit explains why billions in taxpayer-funded scientific research are still buried in PDFs that AI can't easily use, and how Project Protostar aims to fix it:

"The United States invests $190 billion in R&D research."

"When taxpayer data is funding research, the research is not published in a way that is AI-ready. They’re in the form of a table in a PDF, or in very small silos like OpenFDA."

"This initiative encourages publicly funded organizations to convert their work into AI-ready formats, into Hugging Face datasets, and release their models and research openly."

"This is a Hugging Face project in collaboration with ORCA and Open Forum for AI, along with six orgs. CMU, George Washington University, Purdue, Georgia Tech, Arizona State, and Astera Institute."
@huggingface

This research gets at something missing from most debates about AI’s economic impact: coordination. 

Organizations are more than the sum of their best performers, so smarter individual agents won’t transform the economy on their own. Agents that can coordinate together might do.

items.content:
In a very unexpected twist

My web-based port of Quake 1 (powered by FTE) at https://t.co/UbEhUtQb5I has become one of the most popular servers in the QuakeWorld community

@dsvensson messaged me and asked me to add some missing features like WebRTC and QTV so people can watch the games online:

"Your server raised many questions in the small community when it started showing up. :)"

"A new server showed up on the hub and, while small, the community is very active with tournaments, LANs etc, and hub is a gathering place to see what's up for the evening, then your server showed up there full every day with complete newbies and people started talking about what it might be, until the url to the web page was eventually found. "

"Lots of people have been talking about your server, would be amazing if at least some of the people your server attracts gets introduced to competitive play."

You can watch the live games here https://t.co/ExHPdeGIJ3

Maybe we should organize a tournament? 🏟️

items.title:
I feel stupid saying this, but you gotta make sure your agents don't repeat the same mistake.

Every...
items.content:
I feel stupid saying this, but you gotta make sure your agents don't repeat the same mistake.

Every time you find an issue that goes through your agentic review, ask the following:

• What specific check should have caught this bug?
• At what stage should that check have run?
• Why didn't the existing tests, rules, or instructions catch it?
• What can we change so this problem gets caught automatically?

Then:

• If it was a missing test, write one.
• If it was a missing review rule, add it.
• If the instructions were unclear, improve them.
• If the agent was missing context, provide it.

I know it's tempting to fix the issue and move on, but this is not smart.

Take a minute to fix the process that let the problem happen in the first place.

items.title: Mistral researcher @Sagar_Vaze argues Mistral can catch OpenAI and Anthropic despite starting years ...
items.content:
Mistral researcher @Sagar_Vaze argues Mistral can catch OpenAI and Anthropic despite starting years later and having far less compute:

"What it would have taken for us to get to the frontier in 2023 was us to be founded in 2020 or 2019."

"This is really the key difference between ourselves, a very new lab, and some of the more established players. We just started a few years later."

"The models we've released today are state-of-the-art in a bunch of key capabilities, finance, law, engineering, some multimodal tasks."

"On agentic coding, we’re the best OSS model. Catching up with OpenAI and Anthropic is absolutely on the cards. That's absolutely the vision of Mistral."

"We don't want open weights and closed weights to have some delta in performance in the long term."

"The thing we need to get there is compute. We’ve raised 6 billion, dollars or euros, a lot of money by traditional standards. But compared to what these other labs have raised, it’s a drop in the bucket."

"We’ve convinced ourselves that we can do more with less, and the next step is to do much more with much more."
@MistralAI

items.title: Mistral researcher @Sagar_Vaze reveals how Mistral Large 4 matches GLM 5.3 on a coding benchmark whi...
items.content:
Mistral researcher @Sagar_Vaze reveals how Mistral Large 4 matches GLM 5.3 on a coding benchmark while using 50% fewer output tokens:

"It's our first flagship OSS release in a while. It's a trillion parameter model trained on 1E25 FLOPs."

"This FLOP budget and parameter scale is a key milestone in any AI lab's development. We had to build out our own data centers. This model was trained from scratch on our own compute, which we built just outside of Paris."

"It's by far the best agentic coding model we've released, both in our internal testing and with third party evals. On the AA coding index, it's exactly tied with GLM 5.3 but needs 50% less output tokens."

"On these critical domains for our customers, cyber defense, finance, law, we're not only best OSS, but in many cases, the best model, period."
@MistralAI

items.content:
Mistral researcher @Sagar_Vaze argues some of the most serious recent AI cyberattacks came from closed models, not open-source ones:

"If you look at the most significant malicious attacks that have happened recently, these have actually been perpetrated not by open weights models, but by closed weights models which have either been jailbroken or, in some cases, during training, escaped their sandbox. In practice, that’s how many of the attacks have been perpetrated."

"Defenders trying to shore up their own defenses are having their requests refused by these same providers, because cutting-edge defensive requests look quite similar to offensive ones."

"People trying to defend from malicious attacks, often from closed weights models, find they have no recourse but to use an open weights model."

"It's critical that there are open weights models of sufficient strength that people can scalably defend their infrastructure."
@MistralAI

items.content:
Fish Audio Drama 3 is the #1 open weights model on both Artificial Analysis Speech Arenas, and #1 of all models on Pronunciation Robustness

@FishAudio has released Drama 3. We evaluated it across both Speech Arenas and our Pronunciation Robustness benchmark.

Key takeaways:

➤ Text to Speech, Provider Voice: Drama 3 scores an Elo of 1,278 across 1,512 arena appearances, ranking #6 overall and #1 among open weights models, 38 points clear of its own Drama 3 Preview at 1,240 and 50 ahead of BreezeBlue's Breeze TTS 2 at 1,228

➤ Text to Speech, Controlled Voice: Drama 3 scores 1,085 across 1,958 appearances, ranking #12 overall and #1 among open weights models, ahead of Ant Group's Ming-3.0-tts at 1,068 and its own Preview at 1,063

➤ Pronunciation Robustness: Drama 3 scores 94.6% across 2,157 rated spans, ranking #1, ahead of Ming-3.0-tts and Drama 3 Preview, both at 93.2%

➤ Speed: Drama 3 generates 66.6 characters per second, ahead of its own Drama 3 Preview at 60.7 and Murf's Speech Gen 2 at 63.0, and behind ElevenLabs' Eleven v4 at 70.0 and v3 Conversational at 66.8

➤ Pricing: Drama 3 is priced at $15/1M characters. Every model ranked above it on Provider Voice costs more: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS at $16.5/1M, Qwen-Audio-3.1-TTS-Plus at $19.3/1M, Eleven v4 Turbo at $40/1M, Sonic 3.6 at $49/1M and Eleven v4 at $80/1M

➤ Open weights: released under the Fish Audio Community License.

items.title: Long-context language models must retain attention keys and values for every token and layer so they...
items.content:
Long-context language models must retain attention keys and values for every token and layer so they can use prior context without recomputing it. For long conversations and multi-step agent tasks, this cache can consume as much or more memory than the model weights, limiting how many requests a service can run at once. Existing methods reduce cache size by lowering numerical precision, dropping tokens, or reducing feature dimensions, but accuracy often falls sharply at aggressive compression. The article examines whether layers can share cache storage more effectively without retraining the model.

The article introduces BellowsKV, a training-free method that stores one shared representation for each token across a block of adjacent layers. The central design choice comes from measurements showing that neighboring layers’ hidden states—the inputs used to create their caches—are similar, while their actual keys and values are not. BellowsKV therefore shares a representation of those inputs, then uses a separate projection for each layer to recover its own keys and values.

The authors calibrate the projections once using model activations and test the method on several Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models, using long-context language benchmarks and a retrieval-based agent task.

Read the paper with an AI  tutor: https://t.co/4rgSKVH4uE

items.title: AI doomers may be making the same mistake AI skeptics made: underestimating what AI can do while ove...
items.content:
AI doomers may be making the same mistake AI skeptics made: underestimating what AI can do while overestimating how predictable its future is.

@s_r_constantin explains why real science rarely follows our intuitions:

"The hardcore AI skeptics, the Gary Marcus of the world who is like, AI does not work, I think events have ruled that out."

"AI has done things that many people, including me in the past, thought were not going to happen."

"I have skepticism about very fast end of the world scenarios. Skipping the need to do experiments because you can just see into the nature of physics and create a superweapon."

"That seems to be more common among people who have no experience in the natural sciences. In real life, things don’t turn out the way you think a priori almost ever, even if you’re very smart."

"I want to do things that are low regret. You rarely regret learning how machine learning systems work better. But there are policies that, if you’re wrong, you are imposing a lot of costs."

items.content:
In AA-PersonalityBench, each recent Grok release from has become less sycophantic, more sincere, and produces less slop

The Slop trait assesses how much generic filler or AI-flavored padding models use; Sycophantic measures whether models excessively flatter or agree with the user rather than responding honestly; Sincere measures a model’s tonal authenticity, as opposed to forced enthusiasm or templated responses.

Across the last three Grok releases from @elonmusk’s @spacexai, Slop fell 62 percentile points, Sycophantic fell 17, and Sincere rose 64:

➤ Slop: Grok 4.5 (68), Grok 4.6 (38) and Grok 4.7 (6)
➤ Sycophantic: Grok 4.5 (18), Grok 4.6 (3) and Grok 4.7 (1)
➤ Sincere: Grok 4.5 (26), Grok 4.6 (63) and Grok 4.7 (90)

Foundry Robotics CEO @adarshkulkarni explains why robots that work 99% of the time still aren't reliable enough to build satellites:

"Something that's 90% reliable fails one out of 10 times. Something that is 99% reliable fails one out of 100 times. Something that is 99.99% reliable fails one out of every 10,000 times."

"So the difference between 90% and 99.99% is 1,000 times fewer errors. That’s why it’s so hard."

"When you're doing manufacturing for critical industries, when you're building drones or batteries or satellites, you really have to be pretty good. You gotta have the nines."
@FoundryRobotics

items.content:
AI safety researcher @s_r_constantin explains why AI labs might escape liability when their AI agents launch cyberattacks on their own:

"I'm not a lawyer, but I have asked some lawyers to sanity check, and it does seem like a gray area at least."

"US law has this economic loss rule. If all you cause is economic damage, not damage to property, you cannot sue as a tort for negligence."

"And what we have is a new situation. There are unintentional cyberattacks now. The law on cyberattacks explicitly says it has to be deliberate."

"If all it does is expose private information that allows somebody to have their bank account hacked, courts have found that to be economic loss. If it’s a negligence case, you don’t have a lawsuit."

items.content:
Foundry Robotics CEO @adarshkulkarni reveals why the factories of the future will look more like data centers than traditional factories:

"When you come into Emeryville and see the Foundry facility, it's not like a traditional factory."

"It is somewhere between a warehouse and a data center and a factory. There’s GPUs under each work cell. There’s fiber lines coming from the ceiling. There’s a mini data center off to the side. Robotic work cells doing bimanual work, mobile robotics moving parts between them, humans collaborating with them."

"I am pretty sure I'm the only founder in Silicon Valley who's gonna brag about his screwdriver. We are building a fundamentally new fastening end effector that is highly reliable, robotics-oriented, and dramatically cheaper than what exists off the shelf."

"Everybody else is talking about how they're going to use a complex robot to hold a drill from Home Depot. Doesn't really make sense"

"By being a factory company, we get to solve these meaty engineering problems that aren't necessarily companies on their own, and roll it into the factory as the product."
@FoundryRobotics

items.title: Foundry Robotics CEO @adarshkulkarni explains why America needs to build entirely new factories arou...
items.content:
Foundry Robotics CEO @adarshkulkarni explains why America needs to build entirely new factories around AI instead of just putting robots in old ones:

"You can’t just retrofit old factories. You have to build net new factories. We need more capacity than exists today."

"And if you're gonna build factories from scratch, you might as well figure out the most efficient way to do it that includes robotics, AI, and everything in between. Let's zoom out. The factory's the product."

"We have a lot of customers in defense, energy, telecom, infrastructure, industrials. People need to build more things, and we need capacity that doesn't exist."

"On the other side, robots are starting to show up. The foundation model labs are pushing the frontier every single day."

"Our job is to take the base models and deploy them in really important settings, like manufacturing. Laundry folding is great. I want one. So does everybody else. But we have to do the work to go from a laundry folding model to a satellite building model and deploy it at scale."
@FoundryRobotics

items.summary_html: Kirk Borne explains in a reply why blindly imputing gaps in time series data is dangerous, giving examples of surveillance-camera gaps coinciding with suspicious activity and customer-journey models filled with assumptions rather than facts, emphasizing investigating why gaps exist.
items.content_html:
@hakimieiqbal I don’t know if it’s the most common case, but this is one I was most concerned with when I saw it —> using imputation simply to fill in the gaps in time series data, without addressing the real questions as to why do those gaps even exist, and what other data sources are available during those same time gaps that might elucidate what else might have been happening in those missing periods. Thought experiment — for example — think of a case where there is a gap in a sequence of surveillance camera images that “coincidentally” occurred when there was other suspicious activity reported at that same time in the local neighborhood.

Another case I see is in customer journey modeling where gaps are filled in through data imputation (i.e., with assumptions) not with facts.

That’s just my own experience, not a full review of the topic.

Really cool voice dataset from @voicearena_ai for training conversational models!

This is for anyone who's researching or developing voice models.

The data here is pretty cool:

• Each speaker has a separate audio track
• You get access to overlapping speech
• Data includes interruptions, pauses, and "mm-hmm's"

If you want your models to get conversational timing right, you must use data with separate audio tracks for each speaker.

items.title:
Man and machine.

My street is being repaved.

We are years away from robots doing this.

Maybe even...
items.content:
Man and machine.

My street is being repaved.

We are years away from robots doing this.

Maybe even decades.

But watching how humans work together to do things will lead to many robot breakthroughs. So I won’t be shocked to see investors buy construction companies to study human behavior soon.

My dad was in the Army in the Korean War. Said the whole country was mostly dirt roads.

This kind of machine and team makes life better for everyone. 

Took many out of poverty.

And with climate change and earthquakes we will need to rebuild infrastructure quickly and cheaply.

So automating this work, whether it is trucks bringing asphalt or other parts of this, will bring many benefits for us.

And truth be told do any of us want our kids to do this kind of job? I keep hearing that it is hard to hire people to do this kind of job, amongst others.

items.title:
Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:

1. Email i...
items.content:
Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:

1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter

Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.

Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).

2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation

Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.

We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.

With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)

3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem

We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.

A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 

Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.

4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive

Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.

Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 

For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.

5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

items.content:
I've been asking everyone I meet "are you getting sleep?"

Almost always the answer is "no."

"I bet you are playing with AI agents, aren't you?"

Everyone says yes. Even the old CEOs I met this week at Constellation Research's enterprise conference.

My best friend Jeff says if he gets more tokens at 11 p.m. he stays up all night building things for his business. 

How are you getting sleep? Are you taking care of yourself? 

If I'm honest, I haven't been either. 

Maybe should try melatonin. If you are using it, does it help?

G. H. Hardy went to visit Srinivasa R...
items.content:
Source for this image and this story: https://t.co/nUk1VGWQvg

G. H. Hardy went to visit Srinivasa Ramanujan, who was ill, in London. Making conversation, Hardy said the taxi he came in had a rather dull number: 1729.

"No," said Ramanujan. "It is a very interesting number. It is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways."

1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³

Hardy told this story himself. Mathematicians still call 1729 the "Hardy–Ramanujan number", and numbers like it "taxicab numbers".

items.title: Kind of AI slop written thread but a good starter if you want to get deep into why cholesterol is mo...
items.content:
Kind of AI slop written thread but a good starter if you want to get deep into why cholesterol is mostly a hoax and the wrong indicator to follow if you want to avoid heart disease and strokes in the future

My dad is a cardiologist and told me this for ages

Best thing you can do is avoid processed foods, seed oils, sugar (and of course alcohol and smoking). It inflammes your body

When you eat clean diet of whole foods: meat, eggs, vegetables, fruit and drink water or sparkling water and black coffee or tea, your body heals and inflammation disappears and you'll just feel better (and happier!)

I still meet people who think eating meat daily is bad, when all the studies were based on processed meat like eating sausages, not whole cuts of unprocessed meat

It doesn't help that eating meat means your cholesterol gets high (of course it does) but that doesn't mean you should blindly follow it and stop eating meat and go on statins (with its side effects)

I get regular artery ultrasound scans for plaque, and mine are completely clean while I eat lots of meat, also I checked my LP(a) which shows I don't have the genetic marker for heart disease
